title: Introduction of Regulations with Advent of Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines
what_it_is: Introduction of Regulations with Advent of Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Machines

sections.label: Domain-specific AV safety testing
sections.summary: The regulatory approach must be domain-specific, with LTA and Traffic Police requiring autonomous vehicles to pass a controlled safety test before public road testing.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The regulatory approach would thus also have to be domain-specific.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: For example, in transportation, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and the Traffic Police require autonomous vehicles (AVs) to first pass a rigorous safety test within a controlled environment before they can be tested on public roads at specific times and places.

sections.label: Mandatory motor insurance for AVs
sections.summary: LTA requires mandatory motor insurance for autonomous vehicles to cover third-party liability and property damage, protecting road users and property owners.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: In addition, LTA requires mandatory motor insurance for AVs to cover third-party liability and property damage to protect the interests of all road users and property owners.

sections.label: Domain-specific safeguards for public interest
sections.summary: Where needed to protect the public's interest, domain-specific safeguards will be implemented.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Where we see the need to step in to protect the public’s interest, we will implement domain-specific safeguards.

sections.label: No specific plan for AI
sections.summary: The matter is hypothetical and depends on emerging technology; there is no specific individual plan for AI.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But it is hypothetical and we will have to look at the technology as it emerges.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There is no specific individual plan for AI.

sections.label: Existing laws apply to AI owners
sections.summary: Existing legislation applies to the humans or corporate entities owning and operating AI, and criminal law for strong AI is far off.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The example the hon Member brought up in the second question around multiple algorithms colluding, the regulatory framework would be no different from today, because those algorithms would have to have someone who had owned them, written them, supervised them and benefited from the collusion and criminal activity and so on and so forth.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, the existing legislation and laws would need to apply to the humans or the corporate entities that own and operate such AI.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: This then leads us to the hon Member's second supplementary question, which is that criminal law for AI would be an issue if we had what is described as "strong AI" ‒ AI that is sentient, conscious ‒ that is, a general purpose AI where it is able to take its capabilities developed for one task and direct it to another possibly criminal task.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are a long way away from that.

sections.label: No need for Asimov's Laws
sections.summary: Asimov's Laws are not needed today because sentient, conscious strong AI does not exist.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are a long way away from the situation predicated in the Asimov literature which is where a strong AI is sentient, conscious and able to understand issues around harm, human beings, the rank order of relative issues between society and humanity and morality.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, today, as far as Asimov's Laws are concerned, we have no need because we do not have sentient-strong AI.
